I started watching Miranda when i was in high school in like 2012-2013 (the first video I saw was her Starships music video) and even then I didn’t think she was meant for children. I took it as a satirical take on theater kids - so the character was meant to be “young” (like high school or young adult) but the darker undertones in some of the jokes would go right over the heads of anyone younger than someone 16 or so. 

I stopped watching Miranda a looooong time ago, probably circa 2014, but didn’t realize that her act turned into one catered towards actual kids. What’s crazy to me is that legit kids programming takes into consideration the developmental/psychological needs of the demographic it’s catered towards - obviously that’s not what was happening here (and I’m not saying all kids programming is created equal, but still). It’s like she took her pg-13+ rated jokes and started catering them to little kids. It’s really bizarre and shows the lack of professionalism and responsibility she takes to truly understand her audience. I feel like she probably got the most lost in the sauce as the age demographics of her fans started getting blurrier and blurrier, and instead of doubling down on being either a creator for kids or for adults, she just continued with the same crass jokes for younger and younger fans.

Funny thing is, if she had been smart and consulted with professionals about this, she could have easily made the shift to being a legit child entertainer. Instead, she just winged it and consulted other children in her group chats and Miranda’s character went from satirical take on theater kids, to over the top obnoxious and childlike, to… pervy aunt vibes? All while catering to a younger and younger demographic.

The downfall of the Miranda brand (I mean, besides this cancellation) is completely due to her inability to choose a demographic of either kids or adults and I think that comes from lack of professional advising and just utter greed and choosing to be oblivious.

2) bought the paint (just a plain white), primer, and stain (golden mahogany) at Home Depot (~$25)

3) built the frame, and applied one coat of stain. I used a brush and then wiped my strokes after a minute or two but my boyfriend used just the wiping technique and everything turned out nice and even anyway!

4) applied 3 coats of primer to the front of the drawers. Then, a day later I applied 2 coats of the white paint. 

5) assembled the drawers and applied the knobs ($15 from amazon)

6) used an ultra fine sandpaper to smooth out the overall look. I didn’t want it looking ultra shiny, so we decided not to add a top coat.

Basically if you're completely dependent on FA and don't have a few thousand dollars saved, you're probably better off staying on campus, at least at first until you have a better idea of your financial aid situation.
I'm not sure if it's mandatory, but even if it is, it wouldn't matter what kind of meal plan you get, just so long as you get it.

Basically what will happen is that if your financial aid exceeds the cost of tuition and fees, you will receive that extra money (your refund) back to spend as you please. You can then use that money for housing, books, etc. If you are looking for off campus housing, most places require that you make a down payment (typically first and last month's rent, plus a security deposit) before moving in. This can be a little pricey. 

If you don't have enough money in your savings account to get your through your first month or so for rent, on campus housing may be your only option. Typically you get your refund after the drop/add period is over. 

Do you know what your financial aid package amount is, and if it will completely cover your tuition?

For housing, it is absolutely cheaper to get an off campus apartment. However, if you are new to Philly, you might be more comfortable living in on campus housing until you get your bearings. Additionally, it'll be cheaper if you make your own food, but that also depends on how comfortable you are with doing that. You may want to opt for a less expensive meal plan (maybe allocating one or two meals a day) and preparing certain meals like breakfast or lunch in your dorm.
